claims.text: The stability of HEA nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and temperature-activated atomic diffusion.
Configurational entropy favors maintenance of a single-phase solid solution.
Temperature-activated atomic diffusion drives local elemental segregation or ordering.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy dominates and preserves structural and chemical homogeneity.
At higher temperatures, enhanced diffusion overcomes entropy stabilization and causes phase separation.
Diffusion-driven phase separation changes catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a single-phase solid solution.
A controlled temperature ramp from 473 K to 1923 K under catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions is the proposed intervention.
Slightly off-equiatomic samples or samples with engineered diffusion barriers can serve as controls to isolate the diffusion effect.
Increasing temperature toward 1923 K overcomes the activation energy for diffusion and increases atomic mobility.
Increased atomic mobility enables local segregation or ordering and causes departure from the initial homogeneous phase.
Below an alloy-dependent critical temperature, the nanoparticles retain a homogeneous single-phase structure and baseline performance.
Above the critical temperature, measurable ordering or phase segregation occurs together with a deviation in performance from baseline.
At approximately 473 K, the nanoparticles maintain a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
The hypothesis applies only to nanoparticles without pre-existing secondary phases.
Alloy-specific diffusion barriers and stabilizing or destabilizing interactions can shift the segregation kinetics within the tested range.
The critical temperature depends on alloy composition and interatomic interactions.

Persistence of a single-phase solid solution without detectable segregation or ordering near 1923 K, together with unchanged performance, would falsify the proposed high-temperature degradation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats stability through 1923 K as falsifying the mechanism, while the boundary permits the same result to be explained as an exception caused by alloy-specific diffusion barriers or interactions. This escape condition weakens the decisiveness of the stated falsification.
